prompt.context: Your client is a very small consumer packaging company. One of their product lines, for which they have one dedicated machine, is plastic bags for food storage. They have 3 sizes of bags: 4" (sandwich bag), 8" (quart bag), and 12" (gallon bag). The bags are all the same width — the sizes refer to the length of the bag. The client is facing more demand than they think they have capacity to produce.
prompt.question: The client has called us in to figure out two key questions: (1) How can they best utilize their current bag capacity? (2) Should they invest in a new bag machine? Let's start with the capacity question. How would you want to start to think about this problem? What information would you want to have?

clarifying_info.q: What is the machine's production rate?
clarifying_info.a: The machine produces 500 bag-widths per hour, runs 20 hours/day, 5 days/week, 50 weeks/year — totaling 5,000 hours of production per year.

clarifying_info.q: How many bags fit per bag-width for each size?
clarifying_info.a: 4" bags: 6 bags per bag-width; 8" bags: 3 bags per bag-width; 12" bags: 2 bags per bag-width.

clarifying_info.q: What is the profit per bag for each size?
What is the annual demand for each size?
clarifying_info.a: 4" bags: 9M bags; 8" bags: 3M bags; 12" bags: 3M bags.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost of a new machine?
What is the expected payback period?

clarifying_info.a: Demand is growing at population growth rates. It is a mature market with no dramatic changes expected. Throughput is growing at 2% due to efficiency gains.

exhibits.data: 500 bag-widths produced per hour; runs 20 hours/day, 5 days/week, 50 weeks/year; total 5,000 hours/year; 4" bag = 1 bag-width per bag (6 bags/bag-width); 8" bag = 1 bag-width per bag (3 bags/bag-width); 12" bag = 1 bag-width per bag (2 bags/bag-width)

framework: Understand current machine capacity: production rate, hours of operation, annual capacity in bag-widths
Determine output by bag size: bags produced per bag-width, bags per hour by size
Assess demand by bag size: annual demand in units
Calculate profitability by size: profit per bag and total profit potential
Calculate hours of capacity required to fulfill demand for each size
Optimize product mix: rank by profit per hour (or profit per bag-width) and allocate capacity accordingly
Evaluate new machine investment: calculate incremental profit, compare to cost and payback requirement

questions.prompt: Calculate the number of bags produced per hour for each bag size, then determine hours of capacity needed to meet full demand for each size.
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply 500 bag-widths/hour by bags per bag-width for each size to get bags per hour, then divide demand by bags per hour to get hours required. Strong candidates will then compare total required hours (8,000) to available hours (5,000) to identify the capacity shortfall.

math.setup: Bags/hour = 500 bag-widths/hr × bags per bag-width. Hours needed = annual demand ÷ bags per hour.
steps: Total hours needed = 3,000 + 2,000 + 3,000 = 8,000 hrs; Available = 5,000 hrs → shortfall of 3,000 hrs
math.answer: Total demand requires 8,000 hours; only 5,000 hours available. The machine is 3,000 hours short of meeting all demand.

questions.prompt: Calculate total profit for each bag size (if all demand is met), then recommend which products to prioritize given the 5,000-hour capacity constraint.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total profit per product (profit/bag × demand) and compare profit per hour across sizes to rank production priority. Strong answer: produce 4" and 8" bags in full (consuming 5,000 hours exactly), use 12" bags only as overflow. Candidate may also note profit per bag-width = profit/bag × bags/bag-width as the ranking metric.

math.setup: Total profit = profit/bag × annual demand. Profit per hour = total profit ÷ hours needed. Profit per bag-width = profit/bag × bags/bag-width.
steps: Produce 4" (3,000 hrs) + 8" (2,000 hrs) = 5,000 hrs total — uses full capacity; 12" bags are produced only if overload capacity exists
math.answer: Recommended product mix: prioritize 4" and 8" bags to fill all 5,000 hours. Use 12" bags as overflow product. This yields $180K + $90K = $270K in annual profit vs. $270K maximum possible from any other combination.

questions.prompt: Part II: The client has unmet demand for 12" bags (and overall). Should they invest in a new roller (cost: $750K, 5-year payback target)? What would you need to believe for this to be a good investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify minimum annual profit needed from the new machine: $750K ÷ 5 years = $150K/year. Then note the new machine would be used for 12" bags (freeing existing machine for 4"/8"), generating $120K/year from 12" bags alone — which falls short of the $150K/year target. Strong candidates raise conditions under which the investment would make sense.

math.setup: Required annual profit = investment ÷ payback years. Compare to profit available from 12" bags on new machine.
steps: Profit from 12" bags on new machine = $120,000/yr (from prior calculation)
The 12" bag demand alone does not justify the investment
math.answer: The new machine does not pay back on 12" bags alone ($120K/yr vs. $150K/yr needed). Additional profit of $30K/yr is required.

questions.prompt: What would you have to believe for a new machine to be a good investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm conditions that close the $30K/year gap or otherwise justify the investment. Strong answers include: demand grows faster than 2%, a new product is introduced on the new machine, spare capacity is rented out, or prices increase.

questions.prompt: The client's R&D team has developed a new 6" combo bag (holds sandwich on one side, chips/lettuce on the other). Assume immediate market acceptance. What annual profit per bag would be needed to make the new roller a good purchase? (Do not discount cash flows.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should determine: the new machine must earn $150K/yr total; existing 12" bag demand still foregone (or moved to new machine producing $120K/yr from 12" bags). The incremental profit needed = $150K/yr − $120K/yr = $30K/yr from the 6" bag. Then calculate profit/bag at various demand volumes. Strong candidates also mention cannibalization of existing bag sizes.

math.setup: Additional annual profit needed = $150K − $120K = $30K/yr. Profit/bag = $30,000 ÷ demand volume.
steps: Total profit over 5 years needed = $750K; from 12" bags over 5 yrs = $600K; remaining needed = $150K; profit/bag at 1M bags = $150K ÷ 5 ÷ 1M = $0.03
math.answer: At 1M bags/year: need $0.03/bag. At 2M bags/year: need $0.015/bag. At 3M bags/year: need $0.01/bag. This traces out a hyperbolic curve (price × quantity = $30K/yr).

questions.prompt: On the provided graph, draw the curve representing all price/quantity combinations where the investment in the new roller is worthwhile. Does this curve have any endpoints for the client?
questions.guidance: The curve is a rectangular hyperbola: profit/bag = $30,000 / (# of bags). Endpoints: lower quantity limit depends on demand sensitivity (e.g., $1/bag is likely impractical as a consumer food storage product); upper quantity limit is bounded by machine capacity — the 6" bag yields 4 bags per bag-width (500 × 4 = 2,000 bags/hr), so maximum annual production = 2,000 × 5,000 = but new machine has 5,000 hrs; at $0.03/bag and 1M bags, only 500 hours are used, leaving 1,500 hours on the new roller. Physical upper limit: 4 bags per bag-width × 500 × 5,000 = 10M bags but demand is the binding constraint. Practical upper production limit cited in casebook = 4M bags/yr.

math.setup: 6" bag: 4 bags per bag-width (between 3 bags/bag-width for 8" and 6 bags/bag-width for 4"). Bags/hr = 500 × 4 = 2,000. At 1M bags: hours needed = 1M ÷ 2,000 = 500 hrs; remaining capacity = 4,500 hrs on new roller.
steps: Lower endpoint: determined by demand sensitivity / price feasibility (e.g., $1/bag likely too high for consumer market)
Upper endpoint: machine capacity limits production; 2,000 bags/hr × 5,000 hrs = 10M bags max, but practical upper limit ~4M bags/yr
math.answer: Curve is a hyperbola passing through (1M, $0.03), (2M, $0.015), (3M, $0.01). Lower bound driven by price sensitivity; upper bound driven by capacity (~4M bags/yr).

brainstorming.prompt: The client would like to find new applications for large (12" or bigger) storage bags. Brainstorm what applications you might investigate for a large storage bag.

categories.name: Food Storage
ideas: Storing large produce items (melons, heads of lettuce, whole loaves of bread)
Meal prep batch storage (marinating meats, storing prepped vegetables)
Leftovers from large meals or party platters

categories.name: Non-Food Household Uses
ideas: Storing shoes or accessories during travel
Protecting documents or electronics from moisture
Ice bags for injuries or coolers

categories.name: Outdoor / Sporting
ideas: Waterproofing gear during camping or boating
Storing wet swimwear or muddy clothes
Protecting maps, phones, or valuables outdoors

categories.name: Commercial / Institutional
ideas: Restaurant or deli use for bulk ingredient storage

ideas: Packing cubes substitute for clothing compression

recommendation: In the near term, prioritize 4" and 8" bag production to maximize profit per machine hour ($60/hr and $45/hr respectively), allocating all 5,000 available hours to these two products and using 12" bags only as overflow.

Do not invest in a new roller based solely on current 12" bag demand ($120K/yr profit vs. $150K/yr required); however, the investment becomes attractive if a new product such as the 6" combo bag can generate at least $0.03/bag at 1M units, or proportionally lower price at higher volumes.
risks: Demand for 4" and 8" bags may shift, reducing the profit advantage of the current mix
The new 6" combo bag may cannibalize existing bag sizes, reducing net incremental profit
Demand growth at only 2%/yr (population rate) means the payback case is tight and sensitive to assumptions
Market is mature — no dramatic upside without product innovation
next_steps: Validate demand estimates for the 6" combo bag and assess realistic price points
Quantify cannibalization risk from the 6" bag on existing 4" and 8" SKUs
Explore capacity rental options for the new machine during unused hours
Monitor efficiency improvements — if throughput grows >2%/yr, payback timeline improves
